annotator.notes: Student initially confuses a projection matrix with a rotation matrix or attempts to calculate the determinant using the vector components directly. Tutor guides them toward the geometric properties of projection.

task_context.problem_statement: Let $\mathbf{P}$ be the matrix for projecting onto the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -7 \end{pmatrix}.$  Find $\det \mathbf{P}.$
task_context.reference_solution:
A projection matrix is always of the form
\[\begin{pmatrix} \cos^2 \theta & \cos \theta \sin \theta \\ \cos \theta \sin \theta & \sin^2 \theta \end{pmatrix},\]where the vector being projected onto has direction vector $\begin{pmatrix} \cos \theta \\ \sin \theta \end{pmatrix}.$  The determinant of this matrix is then
\[\cos^2 \theta \sin^2 \theta - (\cos \theta \sin \theta)^2 = \boxed{0}.\](Why does this make sense geometrically?)

messages.content: Hi, I'm stuck on this problem: Let $\mathbf{P}$ be the matrix for projecting onto the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -7 \end{pmatrix}.$ Find $\det \mathbf{P}.$ Can you just tell me the answer so I can check my work?

I can certainly help you work through it, but I won't give you the answer upfront. Let's start by thinking about what a projection matrix actually does to a vector in 2D space. If you project every vector in the plane onto a single line, what happens to the 'area' of any shape you start with?
The area would probably stay the same because we are just moving the points onto the line, right? So maybe the determinant is 1?

That's a common intuition, but let's visualize it more closely. If you take a 2D square and project all its points onto a single line, does the resulting image still have any width? Or has it been 'squashed' into a 1D segment?
Oh, I see. It becomes a line segment. A line segment doesn't have any 2D area. Does that mean the determinant is 0?

You've hit on a key geometric property! Since the determinant of a $2 \times 2$ matrix represents the factor by which area is scaled, and you've observed that the projection collapses a 2D area into a 1D line, your reasoning is spot on. To be absolutely sure, could you describe how you might prove this using the matrix form of a projection, or are you confident in the geometric argument?
I think the geometric argument is enough. Since it collapses the space, the scaling factor for area must be 0, so $\det \mathbf{P} = 0$.

That is correct. Geometrically, any projection onto a subspace of lower dimension will always have a determinant of 0 because it is not an invertible transformation. Great job connecting the geometry to the linear algebra!
